items.title: 15.5.1 Central Nervous System - Brain & Spinal Cord

source_refs.note: Topic 15.5.1 with its Tidbits and For Information boxes (PDF 36-40); Figures 15.9 to 15.14 are replaced by original diagrams.

blocks.text: The CNS (brain and spinal cord) is made of inter-neurons and neuroglia. Brain is enclosed within the cranium while spinal cord is enclosed within vertebral column. Both are covered with protective meninges which consists of three layers of membranes;

items: The outermost thick layer (below skull and vertebrae) is called dura mater. It contains larger blood vessels.
The second layer (below dura mater) is thin and is called arachnoid. It acts as a barrier between the cerebrospinal fluid present below it and the blood in the dura mater.
The third layer is very delicate membrane called pia mater. It adheres to the surfaces of brain and spinal and has blood capillaries that nourish the brain and spinal cord.

blocks.alt: A curved section through the top of the head showing, from outside in, the skull, the dura mater, the thin arachnoid, the space between the arachnoid and the pia mater with its web-like strands, the pia mater and the brain tissue.

blocks.text: Structure of Brain
The average adult human brain weighs 1.4 kg (about 2 percent of total body weight). It contains about 100 billion inter-neurons. Each neuron has synapses with several thousand other neurons.

blocks.title: For Information
blocks.text: In Grade X, you have studied the traditional divisions of brain structure i.e., forebrain, midbrain, and hindbrain. Here, you would study the structure of brain according to the latest defined divisions.

blocks.alt: Mid-line section of the brain inside the cranium. The folded cerebrum arches over the corpus callosum; below it are the lateral ventricles, the third ventricle, the thalamus and hypothalamus (diencephalon) and the pituitary gland. The midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata (brainstem) lead down to the spinal cord, with the cerebellum behind and the fourth ventricle between them.

blocks.text: The human brain consists of the following major parts.
1- Cerebrum

It is the largest portion of human brain. Its outer layer is highly folded. It is divided by a deep groove (fissure) into two parts called left and right cerebral hemispheres. At the base of deep groove, both cerebral hemispheres are connected by the corpus callosum (a band of axons). Each hemisphere receives sensory information from the opposite side of the body and sends motor commands to that side.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Damage to one hemisphere results in a loss of sensation and paralysis on the opposite side of body.
Each cerebral hemisphere is divided into four lobes:

items: The frontal lobes are associated with executive functions including self-control, planning, reasoning, and abstract thought.
The parietal lobes process sensory information, give awareness of position of the body and the environment, control attention, plan and execute motor movements.
The temporal lobes are involved in processing sensory input for appropriate retention of visual memory, language comprehension, and emotions.

blocks.alt: Side view of the left cerebral hemisphere, front to the left. The frontal lobe (yellow-green) is at the front, the parietal lobe (blue) at the top behind the central groove, the occipital lobe (tan) at the back and the temporal lobe (green) below the lateral fissure.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.11: Four lobes of cerebrum (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.11).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Frontal lobe, Parietal lobe, Temporal lobe, Occipital lobe.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Ridges in cerebral hemispheres are called gyri (singular, gyrus). Gyri are separated by grooves. A shallow groove is called sulcus (plural, sulci) and a deep groove is called fissure.

Cerebral Cortex: It is the folded outer layer of cerebrum. It is made of grey matter (containing cell bodies and non-myelinated axons). It is densely packed with inter-neurons (about 10% of all neurons in brain). It contains the following areas.

items: The motor areas send impulses to the voluntary (skeletal) muscles.

The sensory areas receive information from different parts. A specialized area called auditory cortex within the temporal lobe deals with different sound frequencies. The visual cortex in the occipital lobe deals with information from the eye.
Association areas of the cortex are the sites of higher mental activities. Some functions are associated with one side, such as language in the left and visual-spatial ability in the right.

blocks.alt: Side view of a cerebral hemisphere, front to the right, coloured by area: primary motor area (pink strip) in front of the primary sensory area (blue strip); somatic association area in the front part; somatic sensory and association area behind the sensory strip; visual association area and visual area at the back; auditory cortex (yellow) in the temporal lobe with the sensory area for speech at its back end; motor area for speech in front, near the motor strip.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.12: Sensory, motor and association areas (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.12).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Primary Sensory area, Somatic sensory & association area, Visual association area, Visual area, Primary motor area, Somatic Association area, Motor area for speech, Sensory area for speech, Auditory cortex.

blocks.text: Below cerebral cortex is the white matter (composed of myelinated axons). It links specific regions of the cortex with each other and with other neural centres.
2- Brainstem
The cerebrum is connected to the spinal cord through brainstem. This region lies below the cerebrum and consists of three main divisions:

items: Midbrain: It relays visual and auditory information. It also contains reticular formation, which connects hindbrain with forebrain.
Pons: It transmits impulses between the cerebral hemispheres and cerebellum.
Medulla oblongata: It serves as both a relay centre and a control centre for heart rate, respiration rate, and other homeostatic activities.

blocks.text: 3- Diencephalon
It is present deep within the brain's center, above the brainstem and beneath the cerebrum (specifically between the cerebral hemispheres). It consists two major parts:

items: Thalamus is a relay centre between sensory information and the cerebrum.

Hypothalamus integrates the visceral activities. It regulates body temperature, hunger and satiety, thirst, and various emotional states. It also controls the pituitary gland, which in turn regulates many of the other endocrine glands.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: The pineal gland is located where the two halves of the thalamus join. It produces a hormone melatonin which controls sleep patterns.
Limbic system

It is a group of linked structures. It lies on both sides of the thalamus, just under the cerebrum. It includes the hypothalamus, the amygdala, the hippocampus, and several other nearby areas. The amygdalae (singular: amygdala) are two almond-shaped structures present deep within the temporal lobes. They control feeling and emotions of love, hate, anger, fear, rage and sexual arousal. The hippocampus consists of two "horns" that curve back from the amygdala. It plays role in the consolidation of information from short-term memory to long-term memory.

blocks.alt: Mid-line section of the brain showing the limbic system: the hypothalamus (green) below the front of the thalamus, the almond-shaped amygdala deep in the temporal lobe (circled), and the hippocampus curving back from it, with the fornix arching over the thalamus.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.13: Limbic system (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.13).

blocks.text: 4- Cerebellum

It is the second major structure in brain. It lies below and behind the cerebral hemispheres. It coordinates muscle actions. It consists of a tightly folded layer of cortex, with white matter underneath. It receives sensory impulses from muscles, tendons, joints, eyes, and ears. It also receives information from other brain centres. It processes information about body position and controls posture. The cerebellum coordinates rapid and ongoing movements. It acts with the brainstem and with the cerebral cortex to coordinate skeletal muscles.
Ventricles of Brain

The brain and spinal cord are hollow structure. It means that they contain fluid-filled cavities called ventricles. There are four ventricles in human brain. There are two large lateral ventricles in cerebrum. The third ventricle is in diencephalon between the right and left thalamus. The fourth ventricle is located between the cerebellum and the brainstem, and it is continuous with the central canal of spinal cord. The main function of ventricles is the production and circulation of cerebrospinal fluid.
Structure of Spinal Cord

The spinal cord is a cable of neurons extending from the medulla oblongata of brain down through the backbone. It is enclosed and protected by the vertebral column and layers of meninges. Like brain, the neurons and neuroglia of spinal cord make grey and white matter, but the arrangement of grey and white matter in spinal cord is opposite to that of brain.

blocks.alt: Cross-section of the spinal cord with an H-shaped grey matter core in white matter, and on each side a dorsal root with a ganglion and a ventral root joining into a spinal nerve. A sensory neuron (pink) runs in from the receptors through the ganglion and dorsal root to an interneuron in the grey matter; a motor neuron (blue) runs out through the ventral root and spinal nerve to the effectors.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.14: Structure of spinal cord and Spinal nerves (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.14).

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: The diameter of spinal cord is between 0.25 to 0.5 inch. It is wider in cervical and lumbar regions. In cervical region, it deals with sensory input and motor output for arms and trunk. In lumbar region, it handles sensory input and motor output for legs.

There are two zones inside spinal cord. The inner H-shaped or butterfly-shaped zone is made of grey matter. It contains cell bodies of inter-neurons and motor neurons. It also contains neuroglia cells and non-myelinated axons. The outer zone is made of white matter. It contains myelinated axons. The inner zone also contains a central fluid-filled canal. It is a continuation of the fourth ventricle of brain. Spinal cord acts as information highway on which messages are transmitted between body and the brain.
